Dolby Vision key concepts

What BL, EL, the DV profiles, the CM versions and the levels are. Every figure cross-checked against primary sources (dovi_tool, Dolby Professional, Netflix Partner docs, Wikipedia).

In this section BL + EL + RPU layers FEL vs MEL Profiles CMv2.9 vs CMv4.0 Levels L0-L11

The three pieces of Dolby Vision: BL, EL and RPU

A Dolby Vision stream always has a base HEVC video + tone-mapping metadata. Some profiles add an extra layer.

PieceWhat it isTypical size
BL · Base Layer10-bit HEVC video. In profiles 7/8 it is valid HDR10 (it looks right on any HDR TV). In profile 5 it is proprietary IPT/ICtCp — it only looks right on DV gear.30-50 GB (2h UHD)
EL · Enhancement LayerOnly in dual-layer profiles (4/7). It holds color and luma residuals that, combined with the BL, reconstruct an internal grading of up to 12-bit 4:2:0.MEL: negligible · FEL: 10-15% of the BL (typically 1-6 Mbps)
RPU · Reference Processing UnitDynamic per-scene tone-mapping metadata (L0-L11). It is interleaved as NAL units in the HEVC stream. It is the DV "brain".< 10 MB typically
Important correction: the legend that "FEL reaches 4000 nits and MEL only 1000" is a community misunderstanding — both carry the same 0-10,000 nit PQ range in L1. What FEL really adds is color and gradient precision (effective bits, not a brightness ceiling).

FEL vs MEL — the real difference

VariantWhat the EL holdsWhat it adds
FEL · Full ELReal luma and chroma residuals, point by point against the BL.12-bit 4:2:0 reconstruction. Finer gradients, less banding, better chroma in saturated scenes.
MEL · Minimal ELAn "empty" EL — structural metadata only, with zero offsets.Nothing perceptible. Functionally equivalent to a Profile 8.1 with container overhead.
Why FEL playback is a delicate matter:

Processing FEL for real means combining BL + EL frame by frame and applying the RPU with dynamic tone-mapping in real time. It costs more compute than HDR10 or single-layer DV, and it requires a Dolby license (Dolby does not release the decoder — every manufacturer integrates a closed SDK). That explains why most of the streaming ecosystem (Apple TV 4K, NVIDIA Shield, FireTV) does not even accept Profile 7: Dolby does not license P7 for generic apps — it reserves it for certified Blu-ray players and some dedicated hardware.

Who actually plays FEL correctly:
CategoryExamplesNotes
Official UHD Blu-ray playersPanasonic UB820/9000, Sony UBP-X800M2/X1100ES, Pioneer UDP-LX800The original route — Dolby certifies them specifically for P7 FEL from disc.
Chinese "Chinoppo" playersReavon UBR-X100/X110/X200, Magnetar UDP800/900, Pioneer LX500 (Mediatek chip)Clones of the discontinued OPPO UDP-205 platform. They play FEL from an ISO or a physical disc without trouble. They need the full ISO — not an MKV rip.
Amlogic + CoreELEC (FEL-aware)Ugoos AM6B+, AM6B Plus, Homatics Box R 4K Plus; S905X4/S922X/S922X-J/Z SoCs licensed by DolbyThe most flexible route for MKV: CoreELEC NG 20.5+/21+ processes real FEL frame by frame on P7 MKVs. Without a Dolby license in the SoC it does not work — that is why NOT every Amlogic box will do.
Premium dedicated hardwareKaleidescape Strato V / Terra / AltoProfessional multiroom server with a full Dolby license.
Some OLED TVs directlyPanasonic GZ2000 (2019) and later Panasonic OLEDs (JZ, LZ, MZ, Z95)Panasonic was the first manufacturer to put a real FEL decoder in a consumer TV. LG and Sony do not process FEL in the TV — they depend on the player.
Important note on boxes that "accept P7 but drop the EL": this still holds for Zidoo/Dune and for Amlogic without a recent CoreELEC-NG. They play BL + RPU (equivalent to P8.1), which looks fine but loses the color precision of the EL. That is exactly the difference from FEL-aware boxes: they process the EL or they do not. If you have a Ugoos AM6B+ with CoreELEC NG up to date, you are in the group that does process it.

Dolby Vision profiles — the full matrix

A Profile in Dolby Vision is the stream's "packaging format": it describes how the layers are organized (single vs dual-layer), which codec is used (HEVC or AV1), what color space the Base Layer has (HDR10, HLG, SDR, proprietary IPT), and how the RPU travels. It is not a "quality" — no profile is better than another in the abstract. What changes is the use case: each ecosystem (UHD Blu-ray, streaming, broadcast, mobile) adopts the profiles that fit its bandwidth, compatibility and licensing constraints.

Knowing a file's profile settles three practical things: (1) whether your player can understand it; (2) whether it looks right on a non-DV display (only profiles with a valid HDR10/SDR/HLG BL are backwards-compatible); (3) which CMv4.0 upgrade pipeline makes sense (e.g. P7 FEL can be upgraded while keeping the EL; there is no point upgrading P5 because the BL is proprietary).

ProfileTypeBackwards compatibilityTypical use
5Single-layer HEVC 10-bit (IPT/ICtCp)None — outside DV gear it looks greenishNetflix, iTunes, Disney+ (old)
7 FELDual-layer (BL + FEL + RPU)The BL is valid HDR10UHD Blu-ray FEL (Paramount, Universal, Lionsgate, etc.)
7 MELDual-layer (BL + MEL + RPU)The BL is valid HDR10UHD Blu-ray with no real FEL (most of 2016-2020)
8.1Single-layer HEVC + RPU in-bandThe BL is valid HDR10Modern streaming (Apple TV+, Disney+, recent Netflix)
8.2Single-layer HEVC + RPUThe BL is SDR BT.709Professional workflows — rare in consumer content
8.4Single-layer HEVC + RPUThe BL is HLGiPhone 12+ recording DV, HLG broadcast
10 / 10.1 / 10.4Single-layer AV1 + RPUnone / HDR10 / HLG respectivelyApple HLS (2024+). Starting to show up in AV1 streaming.
4 (legacy)Dual-layer HEVC with an SDR BT.709 BLYes, to SDRA mastering legacy. Not seen in consumer content today.
Technical note: Profile 7 is not officially valid in .mkv or .mp4 containers according to Dolby — the native container is UHD Blu-ray (.m2ts). mkvmerge accepts it by community convention, and the whole open-source ecosystem (dovi_tool, MadVR, Jellyfin) has adopted that convention.

CM versions — v2.9 and v4.0

Content Mapping is the algorithm that translates the HDR master to the dynamic range of the final TV. It is the metadata that tells the TV how to squeeze the master's 4000+ nits into the ~700-2000 nits it can handle.

VersionIntroducedLevels includedKey changes
CMv2.9Initial (2014-2015)L0-L6"Classic" tone-mapping by 100/300/600/1000 nit target via L2
CMv4.0Autumn 2018 (official docs Dec 2019)L0-L6 + L3, L8, L9, L10, L11L8 functionally replaces L2 with 8 fine parameters. L3 adds dynamic offsets to L1. L11 adds "Content Type" (Movie/Game/Sport/UGC) → Dolby Vision IQ.
CMv4.0 is a superset of CMv2.9, not a replacement: a CMv4.0 RPU still carries L0-L6 in full. TVs without a CMv4.0 engine silently ignore L8-L11 and use L1+L2 as always — nothing breaks, they just do not get the refinement.
Adoption on discs: most pre-2020 UHD BDs are CMv2.9. Recent studios vary — even in 2024-2025 CMv2.9 BDs are still being released. That is where the CMv4.0 upgrade makes sense: the FEL BD is kept and only the RPU is replaced.

Levels L0-L11 — verified specification

LevelNameCMMandatoryPurpose
L0Mastering & Target Display Characteristicsv2.9 + v4.0YesStatic. Mastering display info, aspect ratio, frame rate, algorithm/trim version.
L1Image Character Analysis (Min/Mid/Max)v2.9 + v4.0Yes (every shot)Dynamic. Three values per shot (min, mid, max) in LMS space. It is the basis of tone-mapping.
L2Backwards-compatible trims per target displayv2.9 + v4.0OptionalDynamic. Per-shot trims (Lift, Gain, Gamma, Saturation, Chroma Weight) for 100/300/600/1000/2000/4000 nit displays.
L3L1 offsetsv4.0OptionalDynamic. Min/Mid/Max offsets that are added to L1.
L4Smoothing filtersv2.9 + v4.0OptionalDynamic. Smoothing between shots. Rarely used by colorists in practice.
L5Aspect Ratio / Active Areav2.9 + v4.0OptionalDynamic. Canvas + left/right/top/bottom offsets. Critical in CinemaScope so the TV does not clip luminance in the black bars.
L6MaxCLL / MaxFALL (ST.2086)v2.9 + v4.0Optional (recommended for the HDR10 fallback)Static. The same values HDR10 embeds.
L7Does not exist in public documentation——Neither Wikipedia, Netflix, Dolby Pro nor dovi_tool list it. Probably reserved/unused.
L8Advanced Trims (replaces L2 in v4.0)v4.0OptionalDynamic. 8 parameters: slope, offset, power, chroma, saturation, ms (mid-contrast), mid, clip. Far richer than L2.
L9Source Content Mastering Display Primariesv4.0OptionalDynamic. Primaries + white point of the mastering display, per shot.
L10Target Display Mastering Primariesv4.0OptionalDynamic. The counterpart to L9 for the target display. Public documentation is scarce — dovi_tool preserves it but Dolby has not published the full spec.
L11Content Type (Dolby Vision IQ)v4.0OptionalDynamic. Values: 0=Default, 1=Movies, 2=Game, 3=Sport, 4=UGC. It switches on post-processing profiles in the TV (Filmmaker Mode, Game Mode, etc.).
What the app checks in these levels: before starting the upgrade, the app automatically compares levels L1, L5 and L6 between your Blu-ray and the target bin. If they match closely enough, the upgrade runs in automatic mode. If not, it takes you to visual review (you will see this in detail in the Pipelines section).
L1 max_pq ≠ the luminance you will see on screen. The "DV L1 luminance profile" chart in the Inspect / edit MKV tab shows the max_pq the colorist encoded in the DV metadata — it is what the RPU says the scene has, not what actually gets played. Some discs are labeled very conservatively (Blade Runner 2049 reports a peak L1 of ~176 nits even though real on-screen measurements show ~600 nits). The TV applies tone-mapping and the L2/L8 trims before showing each frame. That is why the figure in the chart can look low for an HDR master — it is reflecting the metadata faithfully, it is not a bug.

why-upgrade:
Why upgrade to CMv4.0

The goal: combine the UHD Blu-ray video (the best picture quality available) with CMv4.0 tone-mapping (typically extracted from streaming versions with a recent remaster). You need to understand what you gain, what you do not, and on which TVs it is worth it before investing hours.

In this section What you gain exactly The levels (L) that make the difference Static upgrade vs real-time conversion TVs that actually make use of it The LLDV case (projectors, Shield, HDFury) Decision tree

What you gain exactly (and what you do not)

The UHD Blu-ray is the best video source you can have at home today. What is not always the best is the set of instructions that comes with it (the RPU) telling your TV how to adapt the picture to its capabilities. Many Blu-rays were mastered before 2018 with CMv2.9 — a lesser standard, with less precision and with known bugs. CMv4.0 is the evolution: same base picture, better tone-mapping instructions. The upgrade replaces only those instructions.

  • Finer adaptive tone-mapping on CMv4.0-aware TVs: level L8 extends L2 with 8 parameters (slope, offset, power, chroma weight, saturation, mid-contrast, mid, clip) — better precision in mid-tones and controlled clipping of highlights.
  • Fixes for CMv2.9-specific bugs: CMv4.0 fixes the over-brightness bug with 1000-nit EDID (moderate-brightness TVs lost detail in highlights) and the Chroma Weight bug in trims.
  • Content type metadata (L11): Dolby Vision IQ — the TV can switch on post-processing profiles automatically depending on the type of material (Filmmaker Mode for film, Game Mode, etc.).
  • The Blu-ray video is preserved intact: neither the HEVC nor the Enhancement Layer are re-encoded. Only the RPU (the metadata) is replaced — zero loss of base picture quality.
What is NOT true (even though it keeps getting repeated):
· "CMv4.0 adds brightness" → no. The 0-10,000 nit PQ range sits in L1, the same in both versions. What changes is how it is mapped, not the range.
· "A dramatic visible improvement" → not on every TV. On pre-2019 TVs it is indistinguishable (the engine ignores L8-L11). On flagship 2023+ OLEDs the difference is there, but it is subtle-to-noticeable, not obvious.
· "CMv4.0 fixes the grading" → no either. If the original master had a color problem, CMv4.0 does not correct it. It corrects the adaptation to the display.

The levels (L) that make the difference

An RPU holds instructions organized in numbered levels (L0, L1, L2…). Each level describes a different aspect of tone-mapping. CMv2.9 has L0, L1, L2, L4, L5, L6. CMv4.0 is a superset: it keeps every v2.9 level and adds L3, L8, L9, L10 and (later) L11. These are the ones that matter for the upgrade:

LevelWhat it doesWhy it improves with v4.0
L1 common v2.9 + v4.0Dynamic per-scene MaxCLL/MaxFALL. The main tone-mapping guide.The same in both versions. Not where the gain is.
L2 common v2.9 + v4.0Trim per target display: slope/offset/power (lift/gamma/gain) across up to 9 different peak brightness levels (100, 600, 1000 nits, etc.).It still exists in v4.0 as a fallback for TVs without a v4.0 engine. On a v4.0 engine it is derived automatically from L8 (and that is why CMv4.0 MKVs keep working on old TVs).
L3 new in v4.0Local adjustment of L1 for a specific scene.It lets the colorist fine-tune specific scenes without touching the rest.
L5 common v2.9 + v4.0Active area (letterbox) — it tells the TV the real picture area.Key for the trust gates: if the bin has a different L5, it is a different cut.
L6 common v2.9 + v4.0Static MaxCLL/MaxFALL (HDR10 fallback).The same in both versions.
L8 new in v4.0 — the big oneExtended trim with 8 parameters: slope, offset, power, chroma weight, saturation, mid-contrast, mid point, clip.It allows trims with far more control than L2. The chroma weight corrects the saturation bug v2.9 dragged along in aggressive trims. It is the main reason for the upgrade.
L9 new in v4.0Gamut source primaries (which color space the master uses: Rec.709, P3, Rec.2020).In v2.9 the TV had to assume. With L9 the TV knows the source gamut for certain and adapts better.
L10 new in v4.0Target display primaries (which space the target reproduces).It allows more precise mapping when the TV has a limited gamut.
L11 added in v4.0 (2020+)Content Type — it signals "film", "sport", "animation", "HDR game", etc.It switches on Dolby Vision IQ: the TV adjusts post-processing (motion, sharpening) automatically.
The decisive level is L8. If a bin is labeled CMv4.0 but holds no L8 (it happens with "empty CMv4.0" bins that only rename levels), the app rejects it in Phase B — it adds nothing over the original Blu-ray. This is exactly one of the critical trust gates.
A nice technical detail: CMv4.0 is backwards compatible. A CMv4.0 MKV plays without failures on a CMv2.9 TV — the old engine ignores the levels it does not understand (L3, L8-L11) and uses L1+L2 as always. That is why the upgrade never "breaks" anything even if your TV is old. It simply does not make use of what is new.

Static upgrade (this app) vs procedural real-time conversion (CoreELEC)

There are two routes to take a CMv2.9 Blu-ray to CMv4.0, and they are radically different in what they do and what they achieve. It pays to understand them well before choosing.

Static upgrade with transfer — what this app does

This app permanently replaces the MKV's RPU with an authentic CMv4.0 one, transferred from an external source signed off by a colorist (retail WEB-DL, a bin from the DoviTools repo). The L3/L8-L11 levels that end up in the MKV are real — with artistic values, per-scene trims and colorimetry primaries a Dolby colorist decided. The resulting file plays the same on any DV chain — your TV, a Shield, an Apple TV, a projector with LLDV, another Amlogic player, a PC. The upgrade travels with the file.

Procedural real-time conversion — "CMv4.0 on-the-fly append" in CoreELEC

Developer builds of CoreELEC such as avdvplus, panni/pannal or cpm —available on Amlogic players with a SoC licensed by Dolby (Ugoos AM6B+, AM6B Plus, Homatics R 4K Plus)— have a "DV CMv4.0 on-the-fly append" toggle that does one very specific thing: when it plays a CMv2.9 RPU, it structurally promotes it to CMv4.0 in memory, without touching the file.

Important — there is no external source: this conversion does not download or look up a retail CMv4.0 bin. It is purely procedural: the CMv4.0 marker (block L254) is added and the L3/L9/L11 levels are filled with neutral/identity defaults (L9=DCI-P3, L11=Cinema, L3 at zero, L8 derived from L2 when it exists). The original CMv2.9 metadata is kept as is; the "upgrade" is only the structural wrapper.

Why does it improve if it adds no real information?

The benefit is indirect but measurable: on receiving a stream labeled CMv4.0, the TV switches from the old DV decoder to the new DV decoder — and that new decoder corrects several known bugs of the CMv2.9 pipeline:

  • Over-brightness bug with 1000-nit EDID: moderate-brightness TVs applied an overly aggressive tone-mapping in CMv2.9; the CMv4.0 pipeline tones it down.
  • Chroma Weight bug in L2 trims: a historic math error in how saturation offsets are applied that CMv4.0 fixes.
  • "base config data" Display-Led DV-STD bug: early tone-mapping visible above all on 4000-nit masters, corrected in v4.0.

So the procedural conversion does not invent L8-L11 and brings no new grading, but it forces the display to run more recent and better debugged code over the same base metadata. Hence the "Auto" mode only switches the append on when one of two conditions holds: (1) the source has no L2 (there are no real trims to "lose" by re-labeling), or (2) the display is brighter than the master's MDL (the TV was going to ignore the trims anyway). In those cases it is zero risk.

Can L8-L11 be "invented" by calculating from L1/L2?

No, not officially. Dolby is clear in its documentation: a real CMv2.9 → CMv4.0 conversion requires re-authoring by a colorist in a Content Mapping Unit. There is no public formula that derives artistically correct L8-L11 trims from L1/L2.

What this app does is transfer L8-L11 levels from a source that does have them authentic (a retail CMv4.0 master of the same edition). What avdvplus does is structural — it fills the gaps with identity so the TV uses the new pipeline. They are different operations with different goals; neither invents artistic metadata.

Head-to-head comparison

AspectStatic upgrade with transfer (this app)Procedural on-the-fly conversion (avdvplus/panni)

What the TV gainsReal artistic trims + the CMv4.0 pipeline (the best of both)Only the CMv4.0 pipeline (the v2.9 bugs get corrected, but with no new trims)
Where it worksOn any player with DV (Apple TV, Shield, TVs, projectors, other Amlogic)Only on the Amlogic box with avdvplus/panni firmware — it is not portable
File portabilityThe resulting MKV is portable — the upgrade travels with itThe original MKV is not modified — the "upgrade" lives in the box

What you have to supplyA compatible retail CMv4.0 bin (the DoviTools repo or your own MKV)Nothing — the box does it on its own with what is in the file

When each one is worth it:
· If your box is a Ugoos AM6B+ (or similar with CoreELEC-avdvplus) and you only play there: the procedural append is convenient, free and enough to correct the v2.9 pipeline bugs without doing anything. You do not need this app.
· If you want a portable file with real colorist trims that plays the same on any DV chain: the static upgrade with transfer is the route. You also gain the authentic L3/L8-L11, not just the pipeline change.
· Combined approach: many advanced users keep the static MKV as a portable "master" and use the procedural append as a convenience for films with no retail bin available.

Matrix of TVs that actually make use of CMv4.0

TVs without a CMv4.0 engine silently ignore L8-L11 and use L1+L2 as always. Nothing fails, they just do not make use of the new trims. Consolidated rule of thumb: 2020+ TVs from brands that support DV usually have a CMv4.0 engine. Details by brand:

BrandCMv4.0 confirmed onNotes

Panasonic OLEDJZ1500/2000 (2021) and later. LZ/MZ (2022-2023), Z95/Z90 (2024).Panasonic was the first with real FEL processing in consumer gear (GZ2000, 2019).

An honest caveat: no brand publishes "CMv4.0 engine on/off" in its firmware release notes. The classification above comes from forum consensus (AVSForum, Firecore, makemkv) and should be read as a "majority trend", not an absolute guarantee per specific firmware.

The LLDV case (Low Latency Dolby Vision)

LLDV / "player-led DV" / "block 5 DV" is the mode where the source player (Apple TV, Shield, HDFury Vertex/Vrroom) does the DV tone-mapping internally and sends an already-mapped standard HDR signal to the receiving device. The TV never sees the real RPU — it only gets HDR with the picture already tone-mapped.

Where it is used: mainly projectors (there are no projectors with real TV-led DV) and HDR10-only displays that want to make use of the DV grading.

LLDV + CMv4.0 = it depends on the player's firmware:
· Apple TV 4K (2022+) tvOS 17+: it applies CMv4 in LLDV correctly.
· CoreELEC and similar: stuck on the CMv2.9 engine for LLDV. L8-L11 are lost.
· NVIDIA Shield: it depends on "Force LLDV" (developer option post 9.1.1).
If your playback chain goes through LLDV on a player without CMv4 support, the upgrade adds nothing. Check your player's firmware before investing hours.

Decision tree — is it worth it in my case?

  1. Is your TV a Samsung? → you get no DV on any model (corporate policy). Stop here.
  2. Is your TV older than 2020? → probably a CMv2.9 engine. The upgrade brings no visible improvement because the TV ignores L8-L11. Stay with the original Blu-ray.
  3. Is your TV a 2020-2022? → it makes some use of CMv4.0 depending on the panel and the processor. Worth it with a retail bin; marginal with generated.
  4. Is your TV a 2023+ flagship (LG G3/G4/C3/C4, Sony A95L/A80L+, Panasonic MZ/Z95, TCL X955+, Hisense U9N+)? → a clear benefit from the upgrade when there is a retail bin. This is where it shows most.
  5. Do you play via LLDV (projector, Shield, HDFury)? → check the firmware. Apple TV tvOS 17+ is OK; CoreELEC stock and several old players can lose the upgrade along the way.
  6. Is your Blu-ray MEL (not FEL)? → consider the "drop the MEL → P8.1 CMv4.0 single-layer" route. Same visual result, lighter file.
  7. Do you play exclusively from a Ugoos with CoreELEC-avdvplus? → you have automatic append in the player. You can skip the static upgrade, or do it only for films you want to archive as portable.
  8. Is there a retail bin for your film in the DoviTools repo? (quick lookup from the app) → if there is, go ahead. If there is only generated, decide by how much you tolerate algorithmic approximations.

Where the information comes from

R3S3t9999 (GitHub handle; also known as REC_9999 or Salty01 on forums) maintains the de facto reference of the open Dolby Vision ecosystem:

  • A set of open-source scripts (DoVi_Scripts) to generate and edit Dolby Vision RPUs.
  • A public sheet documenting, film by film, whether the CMv4.0 upgrade is viable and what to watch out for.

Its retail / restored / generated taxonomy is the standard vocabulary you'll see on AVSForum, the makemkv forum and Reddit r/4kbluray. The sheet is updated by the community: anyone can contribute test data.

Rough size: several hundred catalogued titles spread across the 3 sections (see below). It grows in real time.

Sheet structure — three blocks of columns

The sheet has three blocks of columns, and the same title can appear in several at once: that's not a contradiction, each block documents a different route.

BlockWhat it actually evaluatesWhat the app does
Left — "not feasible"Whether the disc can be converted to P8.1 single-layer, which is what most of the community is after (lighter file, playable on any DV device). The dominant reason — "can only be played on a FEL device and can't be converted to P8 without baking FEL into BL", two thirds of the rows in the block — means the FEL carries real picture information and flattening it would mean re-encoding the video.Blue informational banner "Not convertible to P8.1" with the doesn't apply to this flow chip. This app never flattens to P8: the p7_fel workflow preserves the enhancement layer, so that blocker doesn't affect the result. It rules nothing out.
Right — "feasible"Whether the CMv4.0 block can be restored onto the disc's P7 RPU (the typical note is "cmv4.0 bloc can be restored to the P7 RPU (workflow 2-3)"). This is exactly what this app does.Green banner Feasible: route verified by the community, with a known frame offset and HDR comparisons.
Extra right — "Not Sure!"Bin available but without full verification, or contradictory reports.Amber banner Probably OK: worth checking the sync by hand even if the trust gates pass.
Why the distinction matters: if a title is on the left and on the right, the app goes with the reading on the right and shows all the rows, each one with its source block. It used to collapse the two into a single verdict and the left one always won, so a red rejection came out even when the sheet documented the restore route. The reasons that do lower the light are the ones that affect the result: static dv (flat metadata in the source), mdl mismatch / different grade (the reference master has a different grading) and no bd yet.

How to read each column

The app shows you these fields when the sheet has information about your film:

How to get access to the repo

There is an important difference worth getting straight from the start: the public recommendations sheet (the one the manual's Sheet tab reads) is open and anonymous, it needs nothing from you. The bins themselves (the .bin files on Google Drive) sit in a gated folder maintained personally by REC_9999 — it is not a public link.

The DoviTools community access model

REC_9999 maintains the repository and pays for it out of his own pocket (Drive cost, bandwidth, curation time). To keep it going, access is granted to users who back the project financially. The process is straightforward:

  1. Open the official DoVi_Scripts donation link on PayPal: paypal.com/donate — DoVi_Scripts (the same one in the README of R3S3t9999/DoVi_Scripts on GitHub).
  2. You donate 15 CAD (the reference figure to get access — Canadian dollars, the maintainer's default currency).
  3. In the comments / message field of the PayPal form, write your Google email and a short request along the lines of "access to the RPU repository". All in the same step — no need to write again on a forum or on Discord.

Why the model is gated: storing hundreds of .bin bins (some of them several MB each) covering dozens of films means space and traffic cost on Google Drive, on top of the curation time. The donation model keeps the project sustainable without ads and without going commercial — it is the usual arrangement in A/V community projects when a single maintainer carries the infrastructure.

Retail vs Restored vs Generated — the community taxonomy

Before getting into filenames it helps to understand the conceptual classification the DoviTools community uses to talk about RPUs. Not every CMv4.0 bin is the same: depending on how the RPU was created, the quality of the final result changes substantially. These are the three categories settled on in AVSForum, MakeMKV and the repo itself:

How the app finds the right bin

When you select the source Blu-ray in the "New project" modal, the app:

  1. Reads the filename and pulls out the title and the year, ignoring the usual technical tags (UHD.BluRay.x265, [DV FEL], REMUX, etc.).
  2. If you have TMDb set up, it gets up to 5 alternative titles — useful above all for Asian cinema and other non-Latin languages.
  3. Compares every bin in the repo against the film using similarity matching that tolerates accents, punctuation and variants (II → 2, The / El / La / de, etc.).
  4. Tells apart different films with the same title using the year — e.g. The Lion King 1994 vs The Lion King 2019.
  5. Shows you the best candidates in order. The closest one selects itself, but you can switch to any other on the list.
Provenance warning: if you pick a Generated bin but the repo has a Retail equivalent for the same film, the modal shows an amber warning with the name of the retail bin available — so that you reconsider before creating the project.

What happens when you create the project

  1. The app downloads the bin you chose (5-50 MB typically, immediate on a decent connection).
  2. It computes its short SHA-256 fingerprint — handy if you later share results on forums.
  3. It reads the bin's metadata and checks that it really is CMv4.0 with the levels it needs.
  4. It runs the automatic comparisons (trust gates) against your Blu-ray — frames, L5, L6, L1.
  5. Depending on the results, it takes the automatic route or the route with manual review (see Pipelines).

Inventory cache: the list of every bin in the repo is downloaded the first time and kept locally for 24 hours. To force a re-read, press the reload button in the modal.

The modal's "Local folder" tab will list them. It is a leftover option — the recommended and more convenient way is to use the Drive repository, which is always up to date.

What tools the app uses under the hood

You won't run a single command by hand — the app orchestrates everything. But knowing the pieces helps you understand what it does in each phase, why it takes as long as it takes, and what's behind every result. They're all open-source and they ship inside the app's Docker container.

In this section ffmpeg dovi_tool (the core) mkvmerge mkvpropedit mediainfo

ffmpeg — the Swiss army knife of video

What it is: the de facto standard for video/audio processing. Universal, open-source, inside almost everything that plays video in software.

What the app uses it for: only to extract the video stream out of the MKV without re-encoding it (a pure byte-for-byte copy). It's the first operation of the pipeline.

Interesting find: although dovi_tool (the next tool) can read MKVs directly in theory, in practice it fails with certain Blu-rays because the HEVC metadata is stored in a peculiar way inside the MKV. That's why the app always extracts the HEVC first to an intermediate file — it's slower but 100% reliable.

dovi_tool — the brain of the upgrade

What it is: the reference tool of the open-source Dolby Vision ecosystem. Maintained on GitHub by quietvoid (written in Rust). Every piece of community software uses it — it's the de facto technical reference.

What the app uses it for: pretty much everything that has to do with the RPU (the Dolby Vision metadata) — reading it, analyzing it, modifying it and injecting it. It comes into play in every phase of the pipeline except the purely file-level ones.

What it does in each phase

PhaseWhat dovi_tool doesApproximate duration
A (Analyze)Reads the RPU of the Blu-ray video and extracts its metadata (profile, FEL/MEL, CMv2.9/v4.0, frame count, main L1/L5/L6).2-3 min for a UHD with 155,000 frames
B (Target)The same on the target bin — to classify it and compare it against the Blu-ray.< 5 s
C (Demux)Splits the HEVC video into BL (base layer) and EL (enhancement layer) when the route calls for it.~3 min
E (Correction)Applies to the target RPU the remove and duplicate frame operations you confirmed in the visual review.< 10 s
F (Inject)The key step of the upgrade. Rewrites the whole video with the new CMv4.0 RPU interleaved frame by frame. It doesn't re-encode — it only replaces the metadata.5-7 min (it's the heaviest step)
G (Remux)Combines BL + EL into a dual-layer stream when the route isn't drop-in.~2 min
H (Validate)Re-reads the RPU of the final result to confirm everything checks out: CM v4.0, correct frame count, expected profile.2-3 min
Version in use: the container ships dovi_tool 2.3.2. Key improvements over the 2.1.x versions: inject-rpu places the RPU as the last NALU of the access unit (fixes playback on FFmpeg-based players); mux handles EOS/EOB NALUs by default with no manual flags; extract-rpu accepts Matroska (MKV) as direct input — this lets the DV analysis in the Blu-Ray ISO → MKV and Inspect / edit MKV tabs run without pre-extracting the HEVC with ffmpeg; editor officially supports allow_cmv4_transfer to transfer L3/L8-L11 trims from a CMv4.0 RPU to a CMv2.9 one (we use it in Phase F for the merge branch on P7 FEL); info --summary includes L5 offsets, L8 trims and L9 primaries in structured form.

mkvmerge — the final assembler

What it is: the professional assembler of Matroska (MKV) files. Part of MKVToolNix, the standard suite for working with this format.

What the app uses it for: in the final phase it takes the video with the CMv4.0 RPU already injected and assembles it with the audio, subtitles and chapters of the original Blu-ray. The result is the final MKV that lands in your output folder. It works without copying data needlessly — the progress bar you see in the run modal comes straight from there.

mkvpropedit — instant editing

What it is: mkvmerge's companion tool for editing the properties of an MKV without having to rewrite it (an instant operation).

The CMv4.0 pipeline doesn't use it directly — mkvmerge already writes the right names and flags from the start (video title, tracks, etc.). The app does use it heavily in the Edit MKV properties tab to change track names, default/forced flags and chapters without duplicating the file.

MediaInfo — the expert detector

What it is: the most complete multimedia metadata reader there is. It pulls out every technical detail of a file: codec, real bitrate, channels, HDR10, the commercial audio format…

What the app uses it for: mainly in the Blu-Ray ISO → MKV tab, to tell precisely whether an audio track is Atmos, DTS:X or a variant; to work out the real bitrate; to read the HDR10 metadata of the video. It barely takes part in the CMv4.0 pipeline — there dovi_tool rules everything that concerns Dolby Vision.

Reliability: Dolby Atmos detection (over TrueHD or Dolby Digital+) is deterministic because Dolby publishes the specs. DTS:X detection rests on reverse engineering — it occasionally fails with false negatives, especially with IMAX Enhanced variants. It's a known limitation of the DTS ecosystem.

Keep MKV vs inject RPU — automatic recommendation

Before spending 25 minutes processing, the app checks whether the repo bin really adds quality over the original MKV. If your CMv4.0-capable player (p3i T4 / modern Sony / LG) can do the conversion on the fly at runtime with the same visible result, the app tells you and you can close the project without processing anything. That call is made by a model that looks at the bin data — not at its name or its tag.

Bin quality — CORE / CORE+ / FULL classification

When you download a bin from the DoviTools repo, the app opens it and analyzes the actual richness of its CMv4.0 content — it does not trust the file name or the sheet tag. It looks at how many unique trims it carries, what percentage of frames have colorist work, and whether it uses the CMv4.0-only fields. There are four levels:

QualityMKV tagWhat it means
FULL[CMv4 FULL]A thoroughly worked CMv4.0 master — the colorist used the full toolkit (target_mid_contrast, clip_trim). Highest quality available. Typical of recent UHD BDs from WB and polished studios.
CORE+[CMv4 CORE+]Master with intense shot-by-shot dynamic grading (high combo count relative to the number of scenes). No CMv4.0 extra fields, but plenty of colorist work. Example: 28 Years Later (2025).
CORE[CMv4 CORE]Standard streaming CMv4.0 master (Apple TV+, Disney+, Netflix). Worked, but with infrequent changes. Better than plain CMv2.9, but without the extra fields.
Synthetic— (not applicable)The bin only has the structural CMv4.0 wrapper, with no real trims. It is equivalent to the on-the-fly conversion your player already does. Processing it adds nothing visible. The app recommends keeping the current MKV.

The tag goes on the output MKV automatically — for example Predator Badlands (2025) [CMv4 FULL].mkv. If the bin adds nothing over the on-the-fly conversion, nothing gets processed and the original name stays.

The decision tree the model follows

After downloading the bin, the app answers 3 questions in order:

  1. Does the bin bring real L8 work? If every L8 trim is neutral (synthetic), recommendation: Keep current MKV. No debate — processing it would make no visible difference.
  2. Does the bin profile match the original MKV one? Source and bin on the same profile/el_type (P7 FEL↔P7 FEL, P7 MEL↔P7 MEL, P8↔P8) → the fast drop-in option is available. Mismatch (e.g. a P7 FEL BD with a P7 MEL bin) → a frame-by-frame merge is needed.
  3. Is the bin L2 identical to the original MKV L2? Byte-by-byte comparison of every L2 value. Identical → safe drop-in (swap in the whole bin RPU, ~30s). Different → selective merge keeping the original L2 (rule: never degrade existing metadata).

The four possible actions

ActionWhenWhat it does
Keep current MKVSynthetic bin, no bin at all, or the bin adds nothing over the on-the-fly conversionCloses the project without touching the original MKV. Your CMv4.0-capable player does the conversion at runtime with the same result.
Inject RPU CMv4.0 (fast)Profile matches + L2 identicalSwaps the MKV RPU for the bin one, whole. A ~30 second operation that does not touch the HEVC. Internally: drop-in.
Inject RPU CMv4.0 (keeps L2)Different profile OR different L2Injects only the CMv4.0 levels [3,8,9,11,254] from the bin, keeping the original MKV L2 intact (for compatibility with CMv2.9-only players). Slower operation (~15-20 min).
Force injection (user override)The user decides to process even though the model recommends keepingUseful for archiving the "complete" CMv4.0 version for compatibility with other gear, even though visually it is the same as the on-the-fly conversion. Button "Inject RPU anyway" when the recommendation is to keep.
Multi-player setup: the model is built so the result is correct on any chain (CMv4.0-aware chip, LLDV CMv2.9-only, etc.). That is why "Inject RPU (keeps L2)" does not transfer the bin L2 even when the bin has one — keeping the original MKV L2 guarantees CMv2.9-only chains keep seeing the right thing. Result: both chains see the best available for their version.

What each phase does (and what you see)

Pre-flight — quick bin check before starting

When you start a project with a bin already selected and auto mode on, there is a bin pre-check that runs before Phase A. Its goal is simple: if the bin brings no CMv4.0, abort right away with a clear message before spending the ~12 min Phase A takes to extract the HEVC from the Blu-ray.

  • Drive (DoviTools repo): downloads the .bin (~5s, typically 30-50 MB) and runs dovi_tool info --summary on it.
  • MKV (extract from another MKV): extracts the RPU from the MKV you point at with ffmpeg + dovi_tool extract-rpu (~30s-2min depending on size).
  • Local folder: copies the .bin to the workdir and analyzes it.

If the bin is not CMv4.0 (typical case: "P5 to P8 transfer" bins from the repo, which only change profile without upgrading the CM) → it aborts before Phase A with a log message explaining exactly why and what to look for instead. If it passes → Phase A starts and Phase B reuses the bin in the workdir without downloading it again.

Blocking by design: during the pre-flight the session sits at running_phase="preflight", which stops the auto-pipeline from launching Phase A in parallel. Cancellable like any other phase. If it aborts, none of the heavy analysis gets spent.
Client-resilient: the pre-flight (and every automatic phase after it) runs on the server, independently of the browser. Close the tab, let the Mac sleep or lose the network, and the job carries on to the end. When you come back to the app you see the updated state and the full log in the project panel.

Phase A — Analyze the source Blu-ray

Phase A does more than its name suggests: it is not just "detect what you have", it is also extracting the material that serves as the reference for every later validation. Specifically:

  • Detects the DV profile: P7 FEL (99% of UHD Blu-rays), P7 MEL (the first DV BDs, 2017-2018) or P8 (streaming). This decides the whole pipeline route.
  • Extracts the full RPU from the Blu-ray to a temporary .bin file. It is the heaviest step — it takes a good while, especially on long films, because it has to read the whole HEVC stream and process the NAL units with dovi_tool. This RPU is the baseline the target bin is compared against in the validations.
  • Counts the exact frames in the film. That number is critical: the critical frame validation in the gates only passes if the target bin has exactly the same count (zero tolerance).
  • Captures L1/L5/L6 metadata: dynamic MaxCLL/MaxFALL, letterbox offsets, static MaxCLL. All of it feeds the soft and critical validations that decide whether the target fits this master.
  • Detects the current CM version: v2.9 vs v4.0 on the disc, to know whether the upgrade applies.
What you see: a spinner and the log with the extraction steps. The time depends on the MKV size — from ~30 seconds on a short film to several minutes on films over 2 hours with high bitrates. When it finishes, the app jumps to Phase B with the source RPU already saved in the project workdir.

Phase B — Prepare the target RPU

You pick where the CMv4.0 bin you are going to transfer to your MKV comes from. Three options in the modal:

  1. DoviTools repo (recommended): direct download from the shared repository. One click, no local backups. The app downloads it in the background.
  2. Extract from MKV: if you already have an MKV with CMv4.0 at home (a recent WEB-DL, say), the app extracts the RPU from that file. Useful for cases the repo does not cover.
  3. Local folder (residual): for .bin files you already had downloaded.

As soon as the bin is in the workdir, the app reads its metadata with dovi_tool info --summary: profile, CM version, levels present (L1, L2, L5, L6, L8, L9…), scene/frame count. With that metadata ready, Phase B closes and the next block runs: the validations.

Validations (trust gates) — the decision point

Between Phase B and Phase C, the app compares the target bin metadata against what Phase A pulled from the Blu-ray. This is not a phase (it does no new processing work), it is a decision based on the comparison. It does not appear as a letter in the diagrams, but it does appear as a validations marker, because this is where the pipeline picks the auto route or the manual one.

What gets compared:

  • Frame count — zero tolerance. If they differ, the bin is for another edition.
  • CM version — it has to be v4.0 on the target; if it is not, there is no upgrade to be had and it aborts.
  • L8 present — the level that makes CMv4.0 worth it.
  • L5 offsets — if the letterbox differs a lot, the crops do not match.
  • L1 / L6 divergence — soft validations: divergence does not abort, it just warns.

The app writes a summary of the validations to the log and makes a call:

  • All critical ones pass → trusted. The pipeline marks the bin as pre-validated and skips Phase D (visual review) and — in some cases — Phase C too (no point measuring luminance if there is going to be no chart).
  • A critical one fails → not trusted. The pipeline runs the full route: split layers, build the luminance chart, ask for your visual review in Phase D.
  • A critical one aborts (CM is not v4.0, no L8, L5 way off…) → clear error: the bin is no good for this disc.
Important detail: these validations are possible because Phase A had already extracted the source RPU. If Phase A were skipped, there would be no reference to compare against. That is why Phase A spends so long extracting the RPU even when it looks like all you want is to "detect the profile" — that work gets reused here.

Phase C — Split the video layers

DV Profile 7 Blu-rays have the picture split into two layers inside the same file: the Base Layer (BL) is the HDR10 a TV without Dolby Vision would see, and the Enhancement Layer (EL) is the fine correction DV adds on top. To swap the RPU they have to be split apart. The app does that split automatically and measures luminance levels frame by frame to draw the Phase D chart.

Can be skipped: if your bin is a drop-in (see the case list), nothing needs splitting. If the trust gates pass, there is no need to measure luminance either, because you are not going through the visual review. In those cases this phase is skipped and you save minutes.

Phase D — Visual review (the heart of the pipeline)

This is where the app asks you to take control. It shows you a chart with two overlaid curves: the red one is the scene-by-scene luminance of the original BD, the blue one is the target bin. If both have the same shape, they are aligned. If there is a horizontal offset between them, there is a frame offset to fix before injecting — otherwise the final result would have dark scenes where they should be bright, and the other way round.

  • Presets for zoom (30s / 1min / 5min / 30min / All) to inspect the start, where the offsets from studio logos usually live.
  • Button "Detect offset" that automatically suggests how many frames to remove or duplicate.
  • A confidence meter from 0 to 100%: it measures how similar the two curves are. The "Confirm sync" button only lights up when Δ frames = 0 and confidence is over 85%.
Can be skipped: if the trust gates passed, the app treats the bin as already validated by the community and you do not need a visual review. It goes straight to Phase F. If you want to audit the result even when it is auto-validated, there is a toggle to force the full review.

Phase E — Apply correction (only if needed)

If in Phase D you spot that the curves are misaligned, this is the phase that fixes it. You hit "Apply" and the app removes or duplicates frames at the start of the bin as you tell it. Corrections add up: if you apply -3 and then +1, the net result is -2. If you get it wrong, the "Reset to original" puts the bin back the way it arrived.

This phase does not advance the pipeline — it is a tool you use inside Phase D. Only when you hit "Confirm sync" in D do you move on to the next one.

Phase F — Inject the CMv4.0 RPU

Here the app swaps the original v2.9 RPU of the Blu-ray for the CMv4.0 one from the target. What it does exactly depends on the source/target combination:

  • Drop-in FEL: the bin is a byte-compatible P7 FEL CMv4.0 RPU — it goes straight in without splitting layers. The cleanest case.
  • Merge with a P7 FEL source: the Blu-ray RPU has a real enhancement layer (BL+EL). The app transfers levels [1, 2, 3, 6, 8, 9, 10, 11, 254] from the bin into the FEL RPU — it includes the "common" levels L1/L2/L6 because on FEL the restored WEB grading is usually finer than the disc legacy L1. It keeps the BD crop/aspect ratio (L5). Result: a complete P7 FEL CMv4.0.
  • Merge with a P7 MEL or P8 source: the Blu-ray RPU already describes the final pixels of the disc (no enhancement layer). The app transfers ONLY the CMv4.0-exclusive levels [3, 8, 9, 11, 254] — the per-scene brightness (L1), per-display trims (L2), crop (L5) and peak/max (L6) stay from the BD because they describe your pixels, not the WEB target ones. Result: P8.1 CMv4.0 without altering the character of the disc.
  • P7 MEL → P8.1 direct: if the bin matches the MEL BL (P8 drop-in), it is a clean injection with no merge. The MEL EL is dropped (it adds nothing over a modern CMv4.0) and you are left with a light single-layer.
  • P8 direct: source and target are both P8 with CMv4.0 — clean injection, single-layer.
Why two different level lists: on P7 FEL the combined BL+EL content sometimes drifts slightly from the "static" L1 of the disc, so the restored WEB L1 gives finer tone-mapping scene by scene. On P7 MEL and P8 the BD L1 is the truth of the content — overwriting it with data calibrated for another master would give wrong brightness on HDR TVs. Both lists match exactly the reference implementation bbeny123/remuxer and with the recommendations in the official docs of dovi_tool.

Phase G — Assemble the final MKV

The video with the CMv4.0 RPU is joined with the audio, subtitles and chapters of the original Blu-ray. The resulting MKV is written with a real progress bar, not an estimate. It is written with a temporary suffix and renamed atomically to the final name at the end — if the app is cut off halfway, no half-written MKV is ever left under the definitive name.

Final validation — before Phase H

Just like at the B→C point, there is another gate between G and H: the app checks that the final MKV has the expected frame count and that the Matroska file structure is correct. If anything fails, the MKV is rejected and the project is marked with an error (you can redo it from whichever phase you want).

Two validation routes depending on the mode:
  • Pure drop-in FEL (the typical case with DoviTools bins): the upstream chain already guarantees the output is Profile 7 FEL CMv4.0 — the bin passed pre-flight as CMv4.0, the trust gates from Phase B came back OK, and inject-rpu is a deterministic operation that copies the whole bin into the HEVC stream. That is why Phase H comes down to ffprobe (frame count) + mkvmerge -J (Matroska integrity). Takes seconds.
  • Merge CMv4.0 (when the bin has to transfer levels into the Blu-ray RPU): the final RPU comes out of a frame-by-frame merge, so it is validated as strictly as possible. The app extracts the full RPU from the pre-mux HEVC with dovi_tool extract-rpu and checks frame by frame that: (1) the RPU frame count matches the expected one exactly (tolerance ±2), (2) the metadata reports CM v4.0, (3) the el_type is the expected one for the source workflow, (4) there are L8 blocks present (the trims that make the upgrade worth it). If any of them fails it aborts before the rename — the temporary MKV stays on disk with the suffix .tmp so you can inspect it. Takes 3-8 min depending on the film, comparable to the original extract time.

Phase H — Finalize

If the final validation passes, the app moves the MKV to /mnt/output/, cleans the temporary files out of the workdir and marks the project as complete. It is the only step where the file shows up in its final location — before that it lives with the suffix .tmp so no half-written MKV is left behind if something breaks off.

How the app chooses between automatic and manual

After preparing the bin in Phase B, the app automatically compares it against the original Blu-ray RPU. We call that comparison the trust gates (the confidence checks). If the bin passes every critical one, the app marks it as "pre-validated by the community" and skips the manual phases (D and sometimes C). That turns a pipeline that would otherwise take ~1 hour into ~20-25 minutes.

The visual aligner (Phase D) in detail

Phase D is the most interactive piece of the pipeline and the one that can eat the most time if you end up using it. It only shows up when the bin is not pre-validated by the community, or when you explicitly asked to review even though it is. Its point is that you confirm with your own eyes that the bin is aligned frame by frame with the Blu-ray before injecting — because if there is an offset, the final result would have scenes with the trims applied to the wrong frame.

What the chart shows

  • Horizontal axis: frame number in the film (from 0 to the total — on a 2-hour film at 24 fps that is ~170,000).
  • Vertical axis: maximum luminance per frame (how high the brightness peak gets in that scene).
  • Red curve: the scenes of the original Blu-ray.
  • Blue curve: the scenes of the target bin.
  • Visual goal: both curves have the same shape and are perfectly overlaid. Any horizontal shift between them means a frame offset.

The confidence meter

Below the chart there is a 0 to 100% indicator. It measures how similar the two curves are with a statistical method that has one important property: it only cares about the shape of the curves, not their absolute values. That matters because:

  • A CMv4.0 bin can have different luminance values from the original v2.9 (another grading, another mastering). If the meter looked at absolute values, it would flag them as "different" when in fact they are perfectly aligned in time.
  • Because it only looks at shape, it catches time offsets precisely: with a 5-frame offset, confidence collapses.
  • From 85% up, the app treats the alignment as plausible and lets you confirm.
Two conditions to move on: Δ frames exactly 0 and confidence ≥ 85%. With only one of the two, the "Confirm" button stays disabled and tells you which one is failing.

TMDb — already set up

The Movie Database is a community movie database with a free public API. The app ships with its own key, registered for it, so the movie card, the episode mapping and the ES→EN translation work from the first boot without you signing up anywhere. In Settings you will see the TMDb section marked as app key.

When to put in your own?

In two cases, and neither of them is "to save quota":

  • If the app's key stops working. That is the real reason. A key shipped inside a public application can end up revoked, and the symptom would be cards no longer showing up and series search returning nothing. To settle it: open Settings and press Test on TMDb with the field empty — with the field empty it tests the active key and tells you whether it is still alive.
  • If you would rather your queries went to your own account. A legitimate preference, although TMDb publishes nothing about what you look up.
Usage is not a reason. Measured on a real installation with five months of heavy use: 511 requests that did not come out of cache in total, and 43 on the busiest day. TMDb allows around 50 per second and has no daily quota, and everything the app asks for is cached on disk for 30 days. There is no realistic way to trigger a block using the app, neither on your own nor adding up every user.

Getting your own API key

  1. Open themoviedb.org/signup and create an account (email + password). If you already have one, log in at themoviedb.org/login.
  2. Go to your profile → Settings → API in the left side menu. Direct link: themoviedb.org/settings/api.
  3. Under "Request an API Key" select "Developer". You do not need "Commercial" — this one is free.
  4. Accept the terms of use. Fill in the form with real data:
    • Application name: UHD Blu-ray Toolkit (or whatever name you want)
    • Application URL: any valid URL (for example http://localhost if you have no domain — that works)
    • Application summary: Home use to enrich movie metadata in a personal library
    • Type: Personal / Non-commercial
  5. Submit. Approval is instant — reload the page and you will see your key in the same section. There are two values:
    • API Key (v3 auth) — a short string like 1a2b3c4d5e6f... → this is the one you need.
    • API Read Access Token (v4 auth) — a long JWT string — do NOT use this one, the app uses v3.
  6. Copy it to the clipboard. You will set it up in the app in the "Pasting them into the app" section.

TMDb quota

No explicit limit for personal use. TMDb asks you not to go over 50 requests per second —unreachable with normal use— and there is no daily quota. On top of that the app caches every response on disk for 30 days, so reopening the same project does not ask again.

The DoviTools repository and its donation

The folder link comes with the app, so you do not have to hunt for it in the forums. But it is worth knowing where what is inside comes from.

The repository is maintained by R3S3T_9999 on his own: he pays for the space and the traffic on Drive and, above all, puts in the work of generating and curating each RPU one by one. Hundreds of files reviewed by hand. The project runs on donations of 15 CAD$ (around 10 €) at PayPal · DoVi_Scripts; when you donate, give your email and ask for access to the RPU repository.

What the app does about this. While you use the included link, every 20 bins downloaded it reminds you about the donation once — with the PayPal button and the field to paste your own link. As soon as you paste yours, it stops reminding you: whoever has it already donated. The reminder blocks nothing and gates no feature.

And one thing that does not depend on us: the folder is shared as "anyone with the link", but its author decides that and can change it whenever he wants. If one day the repo tab stops listing anything even though your Google API key works, that will be it — and then the way in is to donate and ask for access.

Google API (Drive) — step by step

Google Cloud gives you a free API key with generous quotas. It is the same mechanism professional applications use — the setup looks intimidating the first time, but it takes ~10 minutes.

Creating a project in Google Cloud

  1. Open console.cloud.google.com with your Google account (any Gmail works — you do not need a paid account, just a normal Google account).
  2. If it is your first time, Google will ask you to accept the Cloud Console terms. Accept. It will not ask for a card; the free tier works without one.
  3. Top left, right next to the Google Cloud logo, there is a project selector. Click it.
  4. In the window that opens, top right, click "New project".
  5. Fill in:
    • Name: UHD Blu-ray Toolkit (or whatever you want)
    • Organization: leave "No organization" if you do not belong to one
    • Location: "No organization"
  6. Click Create. Google will take a few seconds to provision it; you will see a notification when it is ready. Make sure the project selector at the top shows your new project (not another one you had before).

Enabling the Google Drive API

This step is critical. Without enabling the API the key does not work even if you generate it correctly. It is the most common mistake when setting this up.
  1. With your project selected at the top, open the side menu (top left) → APIs & Services → Library. Direct link: console.cloud.google.com/apis/library.
  2. In the search box type "Google Drive API". Click the result card.
  3. Click the blue "Enable" button. Wait a few seconds. When it finishes you will see a screen with usage metrics (zero at first).

Creating the API key

  1. Side menu → APIs & Services → Credentials. Direct link: console.cloud.google.com/apis/credentials.
  2. At the top click "+ Create credentials" → "API key".
  3. Google generates a long string (AIzaSy... format — 39 characters). Copy it to the clipboard.
  4. Optional but recommended: in the "API key created" popup click "Edit API key" (or later from the credentials list). In the "API restrictions" section select "Restrict key" → tick only "Google Drive API". Save.
    Why: if the key leaked, the attacker could only make requests to Drive, not to other Google APIs. It is good security practice.

Google Drive API quota

Generous free tier for personal use:

  • 1,000 requests per 100 seconds per user (~10 req/s sustained)
  • 20,000 requests/day for reads

The app's typical use (opening the new-project modal a dozen times a day, downloading a few bins) is way below that. You will not see limits.

Pasting them into the app

  1. In the app, click the icon at the top right to open the Settings modal.
  2. You can skip TMDb — it already comes configured. If you want to use your own, paste the short string (v3 auth) from the previous step and press "Test"; with the field empty that same button checks the app's key.
  3. In "Google API key" paste the AIzaSy... string. Press "Test".
  4. You can skip "DoviTools Drive folder" too — the link comes with the app. Paste it only if you have donated and been given your own; then press "Test".
  5. Press Save. The configuration stays on the server; you do not have to enter it again when you reopen the browser.

Common problems

SymptomCauseFix
"Test" on Google API key returns 403 The Google Drive API is not enabled in your Cloud Console project Go back to the "Enabling the Google Drive API" step — it is the most forgotten one.
"Test" on Google API key returns 400 Bad Request The key is syntactically invalid (a character got lost while copying) Copy it again from the Google console. It has to be 39 characters and start with AIzaSy.
"Test" on Google API key returns referer not allowed You restricted the key by HTTP referrer instead of by API Edit the key in Cloud Console and change the restriction from "Application restrictions" to None. Use only "API restrictions" to narrow it down to Drive.
"Test" on the Drive folder returns 404 The folder URL is wrong or the folder changed owner Look for the current URL in the AVSForum / MakeMKV / DoviTools Discord threads listed in the DoviTools repository section.
Movie cards disappear and series search returns nothing The TMDb key the app ships with has stopped working Confirm it by pressing "Test" on TMDb with the field empty: it tests the active key. If it says it no longer works, get your own (it is instant, see above) and paste it there.
"Test" on the TMDb key returns 401 Unauthorized You pasted the "Read Access Token v4" instead of the "API Key v3" Go back to themoviedb.org/settings/api and copy the "API Key (v3 auth)" field — the short one, not the long JWT.
TMDb works but does not find the movie Title too obfuscated by the tags in the filename Use the Lookup button on the CMv4.0 tab and search by title + year yourself. The card will show up with the canonical title.

Privacy and security

  • Where they are stored: both keys persist in /config/app_settings.json inside the server's Docker volume, with restrictive file permissions. They never leave your NAS / local server.
  • What the browser sees: nothing. The server never sends the raw values to the frontend — only the last 4 characters as confirmation that they are set.
  • Sharing the file: if you back up the /config volume, you are copying your keys. Treat them as personal credentials.
  • Rotation: if you suspect a key has leaked, generate a new one in Google Cloud / TMDb, paste it into the app and delete the old one from the console it came from.
  • Environment variables: an alternative to setting them in the UI — you can pass TMDB_API_KEY and GOOGLE_API_KEY as env vars to the container. The order is: what you put in the UI beats the environment variable, and both beat the TMDb key the app ships with.
  • The app's TMDb key is not a secret of yours: it travels inside the published image, it is the same for everybody and it only serves to read TMDb's public catalogue. It is not tied to your account, it does not identify your installation, and nobody can spend money with it. If you put in your own, yours is what gets used and nothing else.
  • Going back to the app's key: clear the TMDb field and save, or press Clear all. You never end up without TMDb for deleting your key.
Summary: TMDb and the repo link come with the app and you do not have to touch them. The only thing you have to set up is the Google API key: create a project in Cloud Console and enable the Drive API, ~10 minutes the first time, and that unlocks direct access to hundreds of pre-validated bins. If you use them, consider the 10 € donation to the author of the repository.
